procedure: The teacher boils some water in a tin can.
When the can is full of steam, the teacher removes it from the burner and closes its mouth with an airtight cork.
The teacher pours cold water over the can.
Observe the can as it crumples.
aim: To demonstrate the effect of atmospheric pressure when steam inside a tin can condenses.

viva.question: What causes the can to crumple?
viva.answer: Atmospheric pressure pushes the can inward when the pressure inside it becomes lower.

viva.question: What happens to the steam when cold water is poured over the can?
viva.answer: The steam condenses into liquid water.

viva.question: Why does condensation lower the pressure inside the can?
viva.answer: Condensation greatly reduces the amount of water vapour exerting pressure inside the can.

viva.question: In which direction does atmospheric pressure act?
Why must the cork be airtight?
viva.answer: It prevents air from entering the can and equalising the pressure.

diagram: Draw the two stages: an upright tin can on a stand over a burner, and a crumpled tin can with a hand pouring cold water over it; label the tin can, stand, burner, airtight cork, cold water and crumpled can.
title: Crumpling of a tin can by atmospheric pressure
precautions: The teacher should perform this activity.
Keep hands and face away from the hot can and burner.
Use suitable heat-resistant protection when handling the hot can.
Make sure the cork fits airtight before pouring cold water.
Keep the burner on a stable, heat-resistant surface.
result: The can crumples because the steam inside condenses, lowering the pressure within it. The greater atmospheric pressure outside pushes the can inward.
